The U.S. Army is entering unprecedented territory.
Demand for exquisite munitions has skyrocketed as conflicts in Iran and Ukraine — and an ever-tense Indo-Pacific — continue to redefine stockpile demand.
So, too, has there developed an insatiable market for cheap systems and interceptors capable of balancing scales that, in regions like the Middle East, have been encumbered by cost-per-kill ratios as lopsided as 114-1 — in the case of a PAC-3 interceptor versus a Shahed-136 drone.
If that weren’t enough to consider, there’s the lightning-quick speed of AI integration and unmanned systems into formations, and the reality of having to rethink a simple concept — hiding — that was seldom given a second thought due to the total air superiority of the Global War on Terror.
Such frenzied developments, meanwhile, come against a backdrop of new Pentagon policy that aims to eliminate the antiquated red tape of the acquisition process and speed development to the battlefield.
A daunting cluster of problems to solve, no doubt. But if encountering such a catalog of to-dos is stress-inducing, one would not know it when speaking to U.S. Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal, who finds himself at the center of many of these discussions.
From his office and out on the trail, Obadal oversees the service’s business operations, acquisition strategy, and manpower and personnel systems, among myriad other duties.
Obadal assumed the position after a stint in the private sector, which followed a military career that included time as a Special Operations officer, the status of Master Army Aviator and qualifications in nine different aircraft.
Obadal spoke to Military Times about how he and the Army are approaching these seismic shifts in warfighting philosophy, and how this year’s AUSA exposition reflects the blistering pace of innovation that catalyzes them.
There are many examples of individuals without military experience working in consequential positions within the Pentagon. You are not one. How has your military experience shaped how you approach this role?
What I try very hard to do is not let my experience drive the way I do things. I want it to inform the way I do things, whether that’s my experience working with the interagency and seeing how other executive branch agencies operate, my experience in the conventional military or in other parts of the military, doing joint work, working with partners and allies or going out into corporate America.
I don’t want any one of those things to be the driver of how I make decisions and conduct myself in the business of the Army, but I do want all of it to come together and inform it.
Obadal meets with U.S. National Guardsmen at the Pentagon. (Sgt. Adrianne Lopez/U.S. Army National Guard)
So, it’s certainly very helpful for me when I talk to soldiers or when I look at programs or weapon systems.
The biggest thing it helps me with is understanding that there’s no single weapon system that operates by itself anywhere. They are all part of a joint force, and within that, you have a maneuver Army that is reliant — tanks are reliant on infantry, infantry is reliant on fires, all of it is reliant on aviation, medical and logistics.
All those components work together as a chain, and you have to make sure every link in the chain is as strong as possible.
That’s one of the biggest things that I take away from being in the military: an understanding that all of these things have to work in synergy, and there are no easy solutions.
We continue to watch the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran unfold. What do you expect to see at an event like AUSA that reflects what America has learned from them?
If you walk around the hall at AUSA, it’ll give you a good indication of the Army’s priorities. Our priorities are reflected in what we’re procuring.
Going back several years, when we were in the Middle East and we first saw adversary drones — counter-drone systems became a really important topic. It kind of started in the special operations and then expanded into the larger Army.
Ukraine has not just reinforced that counter-UAS is a critical part of operations today; it’s cemented it.
So, if you walk around AUSA, you’re going to see an immense number of not only drones but also counter-UAS. That’s a reflection of the procurement and the budget, not just in the Army but in the Pentagon.
That’s number one. Number two is software. Being able to see, sense and integrate to understand what your positional advantage is, and understand the adversary and their vulnerabilities.
That’s just military operations, but today it’s looking at how we apply the best sensors and best software to bring all of that together to give decision advantage to our commanders.
The third one is fires, and when you look at current conflicts, the importance of long-range precision fires is highlighted.
So, what you’ll also see at the conference is a reflection of our investment portfolio in our magazine depth, but also the variety of munitions.
Expanding out the optionality that commanders have beyond just one or two exquisite munitions, with everything from longer-range artillery, one-way attack and loitering munitions, up into our higher-end missiles.
All of those represent our fires portfolio, but that’s just for offensive operations. When we get into the defensive side, we’ll be seeing everything from ballistic missiles down to Group One drones.
If you look at those three areas — drones and counter-UAS; software and sensors; and the fires portfolio — and were to roll back the clock to AUSA 10 years ago, the difference is remarkable.
At that time, the focus was very vehicle-centric, armor-centric, pieces of kit for individual soldiers. All of those things are important and are continuing to advance, but these newer investment areas represent a noticeable shift in warfare.
These conflicts are obviously influencing the speed of acquisition. But that process includes an emphasis on both cost-friendly and exquisite munition stockpiles. What is the best balance to ensure success?
The conflicts are definitely influencing and accelerating the way the Army — and certainly the broader Department — are innovating, prototyping, procuring and then fielding different capabilities.
If you were to roll back a decade or even less, you would see very traditional models that go from experimentation into writing an initial requirement document, then into prototyping, then selection, then low-rate production and then finally into fielding and high-rate production.
That’s years long. That process is very deliberate, and it built our military to where it is today, which is still the most dominant, but with a number of vulnerabilities because of technical innovation in the commercial market that adversaries are able to take advantage of.
So, where can we compress this cycle and get it more into a process where we ask the commercial industry to experiment on their dime?
A lot of this has to do with private capital being interested in the defense market. They’re making a bet that they can get through some of the experimentation, and then we can follow on with prototyping and quickly get into low-rate and high-rate production before fielding.
Fielding then allows us to get immediate feedback that goes back into industry. That is essentially what had to happen in Ukraine because it’s existential to them.
So, when we say wartime footing, Ukraine is on the ultimate wartime footing, and there are lessons to draw from there. What are the unnecessary steps in the acquisition process? Where can you smartly accept risk?
Probably one of the biggest drivers of speeding things up is acknowledging that we’re willing to accept risk. We know that if we get a tighter innovation cycle, we’re accepting more risk on the battlefield, but we’re also driving down risk on the battlefield because we’re getting it to them much sooner.
So, then we get into how that translates to fires. Exquisite versus low cost. It’s a balance, or a high-low mix, essentially, where we have to have both offensive and defensive exquisite weapons.
We have to have certain stockpiles to be able to counter the exquisite weapons of our adversaries and have our own effects. Then you get into mass, which comes when we start going beyond the first few days of a conflict, and we’re in protraction. We have to have affordable mass. The cost curve needs to come back in our favor.
While balancing the above, how much of a difference has the surge in domestic manufacturing made in having these pre-positioned elements assisting efforts?
A massive difference.
The Infantry Squad Vehicle is a perfect example. That’s a Chevy Colorado chassis; the drivetrain and suspension are a little different, but it’s nothing unusual.
Essentially, it then goes to a detailer that puts the military-specific equipment on top of it. It’s everything that we need it to be.
An example of an Infantry Squad Vehicle—Utility (ISV-U) that will be used in the final phase of testing being performed by U.S. Army DEVCOM Ground Vehicle Systems Center engineers. (Jennifer DeHaan/U.S. Army)
As with anything, it has its vulnerabilities. We’re sacrificing heavy armor and survivability, which we needed throughout the GWOT years, for mobility, transportability and ease of repair.
But using this model also allows us to sustain it far more easily because so many of the components are commercial.
It especially matters when you get into keeping the ISV — or domestically made equipment — in the decades ahead and needing improvements over the years. With the ISV, as Chevy makes improvements to its chassis and drivetrain, that immediately feeds back into the production line of ISVs.
So, we’re now getting upgrades that are just byproducts of the commercial market.
With acquisition, there’s a major emphasis on AI. What are you discussing with tech companies to ensure the human-in-the-loop element equates to maintaining final say despite the speed of the tech?
Every company that deals with this emerging technology and the military is of the same mindset, which is that the human-in-the-loop factor has to be the default.
There are workflows and cycles that human commanders can say, “I need this to run in the background, and I don’t need to see it or be on it.” But when it comes to kinetic kill chains and making decisions on the battlefield, the workflows that enable commanders have to have very hard stops.
It’s not just a commander saying yes or no. It’s far more complicated and nuanced. It’s presenting options based on a tremendous amount of computing analysis and saying, “Here are all the courses of action based on the priorities that you gave, based on the environmental factors that the agents have been able to ingest and all of the long-term planning that goes into it.
That allows the commanders to then take highly complex tasks like mission planning and distill it down into areas where they can consume it more easily, and then apply what only humans can do, which is context and reason.
That context and reason part is what the tech companies that work with us are very focused on enabling, as opposed to taking over entire workflows.
Autonomy is important, really, in three areas when it comes to warfighting.
Think about combat breaching. That’s one of the most dangerous things we ask a human to do: to breach a linear minefield or barrier. If we can automate that, that removes something inherently dangerous.
The second is highly complex, like command and control. How do you distill what would take human staff officers hours or days into seconds, and give a commander not only several options, but the analysis behind it and the confidence in the product being presented?
The third is the ability to remove repetitive and mundane things human soldiers are doing. Resupplying via trucks, for instance. If we can automate that, we are removing that task from our logistics soldiers and allowing them to apply their talents to solving real problems with a clear vision and mindset.
Beyond weapon systems, something as simple as staging — or hiding — equipment or personnel requires a vastly different strategy than even 10 years ago. How does something as simple as saying, “How do we hide this helo?” impact your conversations with industry?
It’s not something that we’ve had to truly consider as an Army for 40 or 50 years because we were guaranteed air superiority.
We don’t have air superiority at this point because of long-range fires and precision targeting from space.
So, you go back to dispersion, displacement of assets and disaggregation of large headquarters. As you remember from recent decades, a division headquarters would be a massive entity with satellite dishes and other assets in the open. Those days are gone.
We now have to consider how we bring in technology from the companies to allow us to displace 10-foot satellite dishes and 20 miles of wire, and actually have small-scale edge compute and transport systems that can disaggregate everyone. That’s incredibly important.
Certainly, camouflage comes into play. Other classified capabilities come into play as well, and that’s all just the visible element. Then you get into electronic warfare and the ability to monitor.
So, how do you disaggregate some of that?
Those are all things that we are actively moving — and coming back to — in a more modern stance.
About J.D. Simkins
J.D. Simkins is Editor-in-Chief of Military Times and Defense News, and a Marine Corps veteran of the Iraq War.

12 New Hot Wheels Red Line Club Models and a Super Treasure Hunt You Didn’t Know About
17 photos
Photo: Hot Wheels Malaysia
I didn’t even go to the 40th Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention in Los Angeles and I’m still trying to recover from it. That’s because Mattel’s official sneak peeks for November, December and the first part of 2027 are slightly overwhelming.
I’ve already gone through most of them in my two previous stories, covering the basic and the premium models. And I’ve saved the Red Line Club special items for last. Before we talk about them, I also wanted to show you what the next Super Treasure Hunt for next year will be: the Porsche 911 Carrera T! You’ll see it pictured with no wheels, featuring a Spectraflame Red finish and some white lines for contrast.
It will be the fourth variation for this casting, and the third Porsche STH in a row after the 911 Carrera RS 2.7 (2026), the 911 Rallye (2025). If you’re a fan of the German manufacturer, you may already know the premium 911 GT3 RS will be a Chase item next year. But wait, there’s more! We still have some RLC news to look at. The Datsun 240Z will be continuing the Chase trend, and it’s coming this fall.
Phil Riehlman’s Z is one of the castings that can move between different series with ease, despite the obvious inconvenience: it doesn’t have any opening features. It hasn’t been an RLC exclusive since 2018, when only 6,500 units left the factory.
The new Chase Z won’t be as rare as the 2013 HWC.com Special Edition version (3,500 units) or the 31st Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention Dinner Car (1,600 units). Only time will tell what its market value will look like, though.
Photo: Hot Wheels Malaysia You may have seen photos of the VW T1 Rockster that’s also on its way. I almost can’t understand why this casting isn’t more popular. It might be because it’s too extreme compared to the regular vans, even though those were 1/4-mile monsters to begin with.
The 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170 is a new model for Mattel, and I’m “dying” to see the engine bay. It’s bound to be at least one step above the '18 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon, which Brendon Vetuskey was also responsible for.
The RLC Demon will use brand-new Modern Drag Real Riders wheels, which might trickle down into the Car Culture or Boulevard series later down the road. Is this yet another sign that Dragstrip Demons will be returning in 2027, or is that simply wishful thinking on my behalf? The second iteration of the 1969 Ferrari 312 P isn’t identical to the first one although I might seem like that from afar.
It has a new race number on, and new Italian Classic Exotic Real Riders wheels plus it’s inside a blister card and not in a big black box like the first time around. I assume a new variation of the Ferrari 499P Modificata could be in development, too, as it makes no sense for the manufacturer to just release one version of a casting and then simply forget about it. Will it be yellow?
Photo: Lamley Group The 1995 BMW M3 E36 is be the new Membership car for next year, marking the return to Germany after two years spent in the USA (1965 Shelby Cobra 427 S/C in 2026) and Japan (1995 Honda Integra Type R in 2025). I’m almost concerned by the wheels it’s rolling on, even though I have no intention of purchasing it when it goes live on Mattel Creations. Can it truly top the impact the Spectraflame bright orange First Edition release had in 2025?
We’ve got two other replicas of German icons on the list for today, and I’m much too young to dream about the 1972 BMW 2002 . Well, I’m also not nearly rich enough to shop for the 1994 Porsche 911 Turbo 3.6 S “Package” either, but the “math” is much easier in the 1/64th-scale Universe. I’m not saying buying this new collectible will be easy, at least if you don’t have an Overdrive account.
But I’m sure there’s still hope of finding one for under $70 on eBay six to 12 months after its release. The opening engine cover might explain the “BLK MGC” license plate, and I can’t believe I’ve driven one of these in the real world thanks to Porsche having extended that invitation. The Custom ‘72 Datsun 240Z has had six iterations thus far, and there are only 10,000 units out there for the 2019 version.
It’s hard to tell if the new one is blue or purple, but we’ve seen both either way. The 1966 Ford GT40 MKIV is yet another Red Line Club vehicle I’d like in my collection. The lettered tires are a bonus this time, and it’s probably safe to assume we’ll see at least two or three more iterations before 2030. I’m surprised to see that the team in El Segundo chose the 1999 Type R to be the next Honda Red Line Club model.
Photo: Lamley Group Promoting it to “Chase” from the get-go almost feels like safety measure meant to bring in more customers. This way the “Sold Out” message might just show up on your screen minutes after the casting’s debut. You could slap a yellow finish onto almost any car and I’d be interested, and seeing it on the 1998 Subaru Impreza WRX STI makes me realize I was wrong to think Mattel could never top the blue version.
Speaking of blue, we finally know what the Ferrari F8 Spider will look like in the Red Line Club series. It doesn’t seem to have any opening parts, so it might as well have been used for the Elite 64 collection instead. I should follow up on my decision to get some BBR Ferraris next!

ROME — Italy is holding tests with MBDA to mount the European firm’s armaments on the new Astore Levante drone being built by Turkey’s Baykar and Italy’s Leonardo , the head of the Italian air force has said.
The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems, a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo.
The Astore Levante is due to carry Leonardo sensors, but at its unveiling at the Farnborough air show in July it was presented alongside Turkish armaments, including Roketsan’s MAM family of guided bombs and Baykar’s KEMANKES-1 mini cruise missile.
Speaking in Rome on Monday, Italian air force chief Gen. Antonio Conserva said he was not ruling out other suppliers of armaments. “At the moment we have not made choices, the natural armament is Turkish but we also have activities with MBDA and small Italian industrial groups,” he said.
Conserva confirmed the new drone was set to be certified by the end of 2026 or in early 2027. European certification is deemed a prerequisite for selling the drone in Europe.
Mounting European arms will also boost sales efforts in Europe. The Italian air force will initially order three systems, each containing two drones, but Conserva said, “We will see if we go on to expand the capability.”
The Astore Levant will replace the Predator MQ1 flown by the air force, Conserva added. As well as being flown on ISR missions and providing armed support for troops, the drones will also be used for training drone pilots, he said.
Before the launch in July of the Astore Levante, the Italian navy said in April it was eyeing the TB-3 as a carrier-borne drone to fly off its Cavour carrier, which also hosts Italy’s F-35Bs.
The TB-3 is already in service on board the Turkish amphibious assault ship TCG Anadolu. Another TB-3 customer, Indonesia, is expected to base the drone on the Garibaldi, a carrier it has purchased from Italy.
Conserva spoke to reporters on Monday at a conference at the HQ of the Italian air force in Rome which gathered air force and industry officials to discuss the future of warfare.
Asked by Defense News about the prospect of Germany possibly joining the GCAP sixth generation fighter program set up by Italy, Japan and the UK, Conserva said he was in favor.
“We are talking about a strategic partner,” he said.
“We would need to find a political and industrial deal. Germany is a great country. We have already collaborated with them on the Tornado which will retire next year, and the Eurofighter which is the backbone of our national defense and deterrence. Whatever emerges I will view favorably,” he added.
About Tom Kington
Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

Tesla told a Quebec court that car fires are “generally” caused by misuse or vandalism. The judge didn’t buy it, and Tesla Canada now has to cover the C$161,700 an insurer paid out for a Model X that burned in Montreal.
An expert report traced the fire to an electrical failure in the dashboard of the 2020 Model X, which was still under Tesla’s warranty. Tesla offered no data to support its theory, and the court called it out for that.
A Model X fire five minutes after turning on the heat
Owner Sacha De Santis was driving with his girlfriend through Montreal’s Ahuntsic-Cartierville borough around 1 a.m. on March 5, 2023, as first reported by Le Journal de Montréal and TVA Nouvelles . Smoke started filling the cabin shortly after they turned on the heat.
They stopped, got out with their belongings, and within about five minutes the SUV was gone.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Montreal police concluded in 2023 that the fire wasn’t criminal. De Santis’s insurer, Intact, paid him C$161,700 for the car and then went after Tesla Canada to get its money back.
Tesla lost by default, then tried to undo the ruling
Intact argued the SUV was still under Tesla’s factory warranty. In Canada, Tesla’s basic vehicle limited warranty runs 4 years or 80,000 km, and the fire happened roughly three years after the Model X entered service.
An expert report filed with the court found that the fire started on the passenger side of the dashboard and called a premature electrical failure “probable.”
Intact obtained a default judgment against Tesla in June. Tesla then asked the court to retract that judgment, which is how a Tesla employee ended up on the record explaining that car fires usually come down to misuse or vandalism.
Justice Ian Demers wasn’t convinced. He rejected Tesla’s request and wrote that the automaker didn’t raise “the slightest serious” defense, pointing out that Tesla made its vandalism-or-misuse claim “without relying on any data whatsoever” (our translation).
Tesla Canada didn’t respond to the Journal’s request for comment. Intact declined to comment and noted that the deadline to appeal hasn’t expired yet.
Tesla has fire data. It just didn’t bring it to court
Tesla tracks vehicle fires closely, and it publishes the numbers.
Tesla’s Vehicle Fire Safety Report claims roughly one Tesla vehicle fire for every 140 million miles traveled from 2012 to 2024, versus one fire every 17 million miles for the average US vehicle based on NFPA and DOT data. Tesla says its own count includes fires it didn’t cause, like arson, wildfires and structure fires.
For the record, when Tesla first added fire data to its safety reports in 2019 , the figure was one fire per 170 million miles. So Tesla’s own number has gotten worse, not better, though it’s still far better than the gas car average.
But none of that answers the question in front of the judge: did this specific Model X catch fire because of a defect while under warranty? The only expert evidence said yes. Tesla countered with an employee’s impression.
Electrek’s Take
One burned Model X doesn’t make the Model X a fire hazard. EVs catch fire far less often than gas cars, and this case doesn’t change that.

2026 Paris Motor Show • The Volkswagen Group's Affordable BEV Quartet Has Almost Reached 150,000 Orders
The Volkswagen Group's Affordable BEV Quartet Has Almost Reached 150,000 Orders
27 photos
Photo: Volkswagen
Is 150,000 a big number? If we're talking about clocking 150,000 orders for a quartet of entry-level electric vehicles before (supposedly) delivering a single one, it certainly sounds big. The Volkswagen ID. Polo, ID. Cross, Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq celebrated this near-milestone together at the Paris Motor Show, nearly a year after the Electric Urban Car Family was previewed at IAA Mobility in Munich.
The Electric Urban Car Family project has a straightforward origin story: develop a front-biased EV platform that maximizes interior space in the B segment, then develop four distinct and relatively affordable models across three brands on it. Said models slot below the compacts the Volkswagen Group builds on the rear-biased MEB platform, including the ID.4-turned-ID. Tiguan crossover.
To minimize development costs, all four models share their drivetrains and batteries. With these battery-electric vehicles, the Volkswagen Group is targeting one of the fastest-growing segments in Europe, a segment with prices regular people can actually reach. More than 80 percent of the components are shared, meaning that Volkswagen, Cupra, and Skoda did little more than stylistic work to differentiate these models.
Assembly work, however, splits by body style. Both the ID. Polo and Raval are considered superminis, with production being handled by the Martorell plant in Spain. Their crossover equivalents, namely the ID. Cross and the Epiq, hail from the Pamplona facility in Spain. Of course, the Volkswagen Group invested a lot of money into SEAT and the SEAT-born Cupra division to make this Spanish production complex possible.
The 2026 Paris Motor Show wasn't just a photo op, though. This edition was used by Skoda to reveal the Sportline trim leve l, complete with matrix LED headlights and 19-inch wheels. The Epiq Sportline can be had in 40 and 55 flavors, and in the UK, it slots above the Edition 55.
Photo: Volkswagen All in all, the Wolfsburg-based colossus wouldn't have reached almost 150,000 orders for B-segment electric vehicles that (supposedly) haven't even started deliveries without serious demand for attractively priced subcompacts. Beyond the attractive prices, their democratized technologies and versatility also helped drive consumer demand in the Old Continent.
That's 150,00 orders from buyers who are committing to vehicles they haven't driven, and that kind of commercial success is built on three pillars: asking price, the product's competitive strengths, and brand trust. In this particular segment, where margins are pretty slim and every platform decision is ruthless from a financial standpoint, this kind of order bank should be viewed as a verdict the market handed down before the launch.
It's not all smooth sailing, though. Both Martorell-built hatchbacks have been hit with their first recalls, with Germany's KBA explaining that 1,109 units of the ID. Polo may be hindered by a B-pillar seatbelt anchorage flaw . Under a different campaign, the Cupra brand is recalling a total of 10,151 Terramar and Raval vehicles produced through September 3, 2026, as opposed to September 2, 2026, for the suspect ID. Polo hatchbacks.
The Ravals and Terramars are suspected of insufficiently fastened lower seatbelt anchors . Relatively small populations, for sure, but said recalls demonstrate that new products come with new challenges for the people employed to assemble them. Fortunately for everyone, both fixes are reassuringly simple.

Orient Overseas Container Line reported a 45.1% year-over-year increase in third-quarter liner revenue to $3.28 billion, as higher revenue per container and increased cargo volumes drove gains across all four of its reported trade regions.
OOCL handled 2.12 million twenty-foot equivalent units in the quarter ended Sept. 30, up 9% from a year earlier, according to an Oct. 9 operational update from parent Orient Overseas (International) Ltd., itself majority-owned by China’s Cosco Shipping Holdings . Average liner revenue per TEU increased 33.1%.
Cargo growth outpaced a 3.6% increase in loadable capacity. OOIL reported that the overall load factor increased 4.2% compared with the third quarter of 2025.
Trans-Pacific leads revenue growth
The trans-Pacific trade delivered the largest revenue increase among OOCL’s reported regions. Revenue rose 71.8% to $1.44 billion, while container volumes increased 13.1% to 595,139 TEUs. That compared with revenue of $837.9 million and volumes of 526,032 TEUs in the same quarter last year.
Asia-Europe recorded the fastest volume growth, with liftings rising 15.4% to 399,162 TEUs. Revenue on the trade increased 45% to $695.8 million.
Intra-Asia and Australasia remained OOCL’s largest region by container volume, handling 981,336 TEUs, up 4.6%. Revenue increased 23.7% to $947.6 million. Trans-Atlantic volumes rose 7.3% to 147,008 TEUs, while revenue increased 11.9% to $201.8 million.
Revenue growth exceeded volume growth in each region, consistent with the company’s reported increase in average revenue per TEU . The update did not identify the market conditions behind those gains.
Nine-month revenue approaches $8 billion
For the first nine months of 2026, OOCL’s liner revenue increased 18.9% to $7.96 billion from $6.70 billion a year earlier. Container volumes rose 6.5% to 6.25 million TEUs, while average liner revenue per TEU increased 11.6%.
Loadable capacity increased 4.8% over the nine-month period, and OOIL reported a 1.4% increase in the overall load factor. Trans-Pacific revenue rose 27% to $3.16 billion, while Asia-Europe revenue increased 19% to $1.70 billion. Intra-Asia and Australasia revenue grew 13.8% to $2.55 billion, and trans-Atlantic revenue edged up 2.2% to $556.3 million.
The operational update did not include earnings or expense figures.

NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports.
Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine.
“They are looking for a way to diversify at a time when Russia is no longer active in defense markets as it increasingly looks inwards towards its domestic needs, reducing its capacity to export air defense systems, especially in large numbers,” Aleksei Zakharov, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi told Defense News. “As a result, Central Asian countries are looking for possible alternatives.”
Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the sales of the Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan earlier this month in an interview with news agency Asian New International. He did not disclose the contract value.
RELATED
India moves closer to a homegrown, long-range air defense
A recent interceptor test marked the first demonstration of New Delhi’s efforts to build a system that could rival the Russian-made S-400.
By Anjana Pasricha
In 2022, Armenia became India’s first foreign customer for the air defense system.
The Akash system can simultaneously engage multiple targets at ranges up to 25km according to the Defense Ministry. It also incorporates protections against electronic jamming.
Calling the system one of India’s “success stories,” Singh said: “It shows the maturing of our indigenous missile design and production system. It is effective in dealing with high-velocity aerial targets.”
Indian defense officials have said it was used effectively by the armed forces during the country’s four-day conflict with Pakistan in 2025.
Confidence in the missile system got a boost after it was “battle-tested” in a real conflict, according to Zakharov and could encourage Central Asian buyers to consider other Indian hardware, such as artillery and radar systems, as growing geopolitical uncertainty prompts countries to broaden their supplier base.
“Certainly this can be an important first step for India’s entry into the defense markets of Central Asia. For those countries, it is also about reducing dependency on any one single source which can be useful if there are disruptions,” he said. “The Indian systems such as Akash are also cost-effective.”
In fact, Armenia has emerged as India’s largest buyer of military equipment, signing defense contracts worth nearly $2 billion since 2020, according to reports. Its purchases include multiple-launch rocket systems, counter-drone systems and anti-tank missiles.
Analysts say India’s outreach in Central Asia also aims to balance China’s growing influence in the region where Beijing has emerged as a major supplier of military equipment in recent years.
India, which has been a major arms importer for decades has been gradually developing its own defense industry and boosting exports, which rose about 62 per cent in the last financial year to $4.1 billion. Indian companies export missiles, drones, armored vehicles, ammunition and aircraft components to more than 80 countries.
Its most high-profile export is the BrahMos, a supersonic cruise missile developed jointly with Russia. India has won customers in Southeast Asian countries like the Philippines, where it is delivering a shore-based, anti-ship system. New Delhi has also signed a deal with Vietnam, and discussions are underway with Indonesia to supply the missiles.
“BrahMos is a kind of benchmark for our emerging export story. This is one of the high-end strategic systems that we’ve been able to export,” he said.

Volkswagen bets on low-cost EVs to beat China
If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em, right? Volkswagen is betting on its new lineup of smaller, more affordable electric cars to fight back against BYD and other Chinese automakers.
So far, it appears to be paying off—at least in Europe. The Volkswagen Group is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market, according to Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss.
Sander said the sudden rush of buyers is due to a combination of high fuel prices and its new lineup of entry-level EVs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has already received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.
The lineup currently includes the Volkswagen ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all of which share the same underpinnings.
Volkswagen Group’s Electric Urban Car Family receives nearly 150,000 orders to date (Source: The Volkswagen Group)
Overall, Volkswagen said that one in five models delivered in Europe was all-electric in the third quarter, with the order book share up to around 40%.
The Group delivered 209,100 EVs in Europe in the third quarter, up 20% from Q3 2025, while EV orders were up 60% year-over-year. Through September, VW Group delivered 586,100 all-electric vehicles in Europe, up 12% from the same period in 2025.
Last month, German auto news outlet Automobilwoche reported that Volkswagen is adjusting production across several plants to meet higher-than-expected EV demand.
Volkswagen Group’s Electric Urban Car Family (Source: The Volkswagen Group)
In Germany, Volkswagen’s home market and the heart of the European auto industry, orders for pure electric cars now exceed those of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles.
The VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery starts at just €24,995 ($29,000) and offers a WLTP range of 334 km (207 miles). The ID. Cross , the electric counterpart to VW’s best-selling T-Cross in Europe, starts at €27,995 ($32,000) in Germany.
While it’s gaining traction in its home market, Volkswagen Group’s total EV deliveries are down 5.4% through the first nine months of 2026.
Volkswagen ID. Polo and Cupra Raval enter production at SEAT & CUPRA plant in Martorell (Source: Volkswagen)
The Group delivered 678,700 all-electric vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 , down 5.4% from the 717,700 it moved during the same period last year.
In the US and China, the Group’s EV sales are down 78.4% and 42.5%, respectively, through September.
“The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge,” Sander said, adding that the Group’s “new locally developed electric models are beginning to make an impact.”
Volkswagen ID.UNYX 08 launch event (Source: Volkswagen)
Compared to the same quarter last year, the company delivered about 30% more electrified vehicles, including plug-in hybrids and range-extended electric vehicles, in China in Q3. However, Volkswagen delivered just 48,900 EVs through September, down 42.5% from the same period in 2025.
The overall EV market in the US declined significantly, Volkswagen said, after the $7,500 federal tax credit expired and import tariffs were added.
The VW Group delivered just 14,900 all-electric vehicles in the US through September, down 78.4% from the 68,700 it managed during the same period last year.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan (Source: Volkswagen)
Volkswagen ended production of the ID.4 in the US earlier this year. The ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe) will be replaced by the ID. Tiguan , set to go on sale in early 2027 as part of VW’s next-generation electric vehicles.
In total, the Group delivered 6.01 million vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 across all powertrains, down 9% year over year.
Electrek’s Take
Volkswagen’s new entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start in Europe, but will it be enough to overcome China’s brutal EV market?
As China becomes flooded with low-cost domestic EVs, BYD and other leading brands are looking overseas to markets like Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia to drive growth.
Volkswagen still faces an uphill battle. Last month, the company’s supervisory board approved its Future Plan 2030 , which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

Volkswagen, Audi, and Porsche All Lost US Sales in Q3 2026

The Volkswagen Group's core brands in the United States market had a rough third quarter. For starters, Volkswagen sold 11,481 fewer ID.4 electric crossovers than a year earlier. Its collapse helps explain why the internal combustion Tiguan and Jetta could not prevent an overall decline, while Audi and Porsche faced their own problems with electric vehicles and product transitions.
Altogether, these brands reported 133,956 deliveries in the third quarter of 2026 stateside. Compared to 152,866 in the third quarter of 2025, that's down 12.4 percent. Volkswagen's total fell 10.9 percent to 78,179 units, Audi deliveries contracted 15 percent to 39,751 vehicles, and Porsche dropped 12.9 percent to 16,026 deliveries in the United States of America.
As noted earlier, the gas-powered Tiguan and Jetta provided some relief for the corest of Volkswagen Group brands. Tiguan sales improved 27.4 percent to 28,091 units, making it the best-selling Volkswagen of the quarter. Jetta sales rose 24.9 percent to 14,092 units, while the Taos crossover held flat at 9,780 deliveries. Those increases lifted passenger car sales 16.6 percent.
The SUV line had it worse, for combined sales of the Atlas and ID. models fell sharply enough to drag total sport utility vehicle volume down 16.2 percent. Atlas fell 19.5 percent, Atlas Cross Sport slipped 9.5 percent, and the ID.4 recorded a pitiful 989 deliveries compared to an even worse 432 for the ID. Buzz family hauler.
There is, however, some context at play here. Federal tax credits are no longer a thing, and the ID.4 is no longer available to configure stateside. Production came to a screeching halt earlier this year, freeing valuable Chattanooga plant output for the redesigned Atlas and Atlas Cross Sport. The existing ID.4 inventory could last into 2027.
Photo: Porsche There is a planned future version of the ID.4 for North America, and that vehicle is called the ID. Tiguan. With a bit of luck, the newcomer should hit dealer lots in the latter half of 2027 as a 2028 model. Audi 's story is a bit more complicated, with the premium-oriented automaker from Ingolstadt delivering 39,751 vehicles in the past quarter.
Several recently introduced models gained ground, of which the A5 stands out for improving 53 percent. A6 volume rose 36 percent, Q3 sales 24 percent, and the Q5 improved by 17 percent. While it may be pricier, the Q7 advanced 42 percent to 6,071 units. The aging Q8, meanwhile, more than doubled sales to 4,095 units.
Said gains weren't enough to cover falling Q6 e-tron deliveries, and it's really bad. The Premium Platform Electric-based model nosedived from 10,059 units to 619 last quarter, whereas the Q4 e-tron dropped from 2,956 to 8 examples of the breed. The A6 Sportback e-tron, which uses similar underpinnings to the Q6 e-tron, also slid a lot. Of course, e-tron GT sales fell as well.
Porsche's decline is noteworthy as well, a decline attributed by the Zuffenhausen-based marque to the lower volume of 718 sales. Both gas-powered models are on their way out for good to make room for the 718 Electric line, and yes, Porsche is not bringing the gas-powered 718 back. Instead, the full-electric version will have to suffice from 2027 forward.
Of the 16,026 vehicles Porsche dealers moved in the US in Q3 2026, the Cayenne was the biggest winner, contributing 5,837 sales compared to 5,519 for the Macan. The internal combustion 718, by comparison, sold 8 units. The Taycan, which is clearly showing its age, didn't fare well. Instead of 1,553 deliveries in Q3 2025, it fell to 537 this past quarter.

CHAOS is rolling out its Mk 0 and Mk 1 VESPID interceptors. (CHAOS)
WASHINGTON — Defense tech startup CHAOS Industries has unveiled a new family of small low-cost interceptors, dubbed VESPID.
The system comes in two sizes: the Mk 0, which is “man-portable and designed for austere environments,” and the Mk 1, which is “a faster, more maneuverable variant designed for high-density installations with a multitube launcher,” according to a company press release.
That multitube launcher is an existing system from ISS Aerospace, a UK company, according to a company spokesperson, who added that the Mk 1 can be integrated with Coyote launchers as well. That’s notable, as integration with Coyote is a key requirement for the Army’s Next Generation C-sUAS Missile program, which the service launched in August.
The spokesperson said that while the firm is not under contract at this time with any militaries, “We are participating in several domestic and international competitions with both Mk 0 and Mk 1 variants.”
The press release also highlights an “[a]bility to operate in congested electromagnetic environments.” According to the spokesperson, that line is in reference to a plan to use CHAOS’s radar transmitter “as a datalink to burn through jamming. In addition, the datalink waveform contains means for error detection and correction.”
Production wise, CHAOS claims plans are in place for a production capacity of 12,000 interceptors per year, with “a manufacturing architecture capable of expanding to 50,000” as needed. Work would be done at the company’s recently opened El Segundo, Calif. location.
The Los Angeles-based firm, which launched in 2022, becomes one of many to roll out new missile defense systems during this year’s AUSA conference, including low-cost interceptors from Anduril and Lockheed Martin , and a host of c-UAS radars and EW systems on the show floor.

The 3D Multi-Domain Task Force, in conjunction with the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense, launched High-Altitude Balloons (HABs) from Won Pat International Airport in Guam on June 10, 2024. T (US Army/ Sgt. Perla Alfaro)
WASHINGTON — After scrubbing a large-scale, high-altitude balloon demonstration in the Indo-Pacific last year to send the assets over to the Middle East, the US Army has gleaned a series of observations for future use, according to a senior service official.
“We were asked to pivot and do some experimentation in combination with operations, and we pivoted and supported operations in CENTCOM [US Central Command],” Andrew Evans, the director for the Strategy & Transformation Office inside the Army’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence shop (G-2), told Breaking Defense today.
“They were effective for the mission that they were assigned,” he added, though he was not able to disclose the exact location and operational scenarios in which they were used.
The Army has tested out high-altitude balloons multiple times in the last few decades, and the service has revived the push to deploy them in recent years for added battlefield sensing and communications. Testing has typically included one or two balloons at a time, but the Army was looking to experiment with over a hundred high-altitude balloons in the skies over waters in the Indo-Pacific in 2026. While that didn’t come to fruition, smaller balloon swarms were used in CENTCOM.
“From a scale perspective, we went from one to two to dozens simultaneously,” Evans said on the sidelines of the Annual Association of the US Army conference. The smaller swarms were enough to highlight a trio of challenges associated with operating those autonomous balloons inside a theater with active military operations.
First, there were logistical challenges tied to transporting the balloons into the Middle East and then storing them.
“Balloons can be a little finicky in terms of temperature, and you have to contend with environmental characteristics,” Evans said.
Then, there were questions about how to support and operate the balloons — something the Army and joint force will need to do “a little bit of additional thinking” about regarding what force structure will need to look like, Evans said.
“We had a lot of help from vendors in this space, but as you think about employing your systems and going from something like a Pacific [theater] to something like a CENTCOM [theater], you learn where those friction points might exist between what the military might need to inherently own, and … what a vendor could help provide in terms of the service,” Evens said.
Given the ongoing regional options, industry had to put the military in “driver’s seat” to ensure everything was in accordance with the proper authorities the US military had.
“And there’s just not a lot of folks that are trained on how to operate it, so we’ve learned some things along the way and we’re going to take those back,” Evans said.
Another challenge, albeit one expected, was related to airspace control. While Evans did not expand on this point, airspace control has been a point of contention as the military seeks to add aerial drones into airspace that also includes manned military aircraft and commercials planes.
“There were some challenges. … That was not a new finding, [but] a consistent observation,” Evans said.
As for what’s next for balloon experiments and buys, Evans said Army leaders are pretty certain that they need stratospheric sensing capabilities, but it is “unclear” how they will be delivered.
“Would it be a balloon? Would it be a solar glider? Would it be some sort of pseudo satellite?” he said. “It’s unclear. No decision has been made.”

Gen. Alexus Grynkewich Supreme Allied Commander Europe, NATO, addresses the Warsaw Security Forum 2026 (Warsaw Security Forum)
BELFAST — Despite assuring an audience today that a conflict on NATO territory is neither “imminent or inevitable,” Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, outlined a strategic “theory of victory” and offered a warning to potential aggressors.
He told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO’s aim is to deter adversaries, “but if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” adding that “any attack against any ally” will end up “utterly futile.”
NATO is capable of carrying out this vision by implementing its “theory of victory,” a classified version of which was agreed upon by all 32 alliance members “about three months ago,” according to Grynkewich .
Grynkewich, who also serves as commander of United States European Command, did not say against whom, exactly, the alliance would fight, but the speech comes as European capitals have increasingly called out Russia for what they alleged are a string of sabotage cases across the continent. Grynkewich said the incidents were making allied populations “a bit nervous.”
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of the alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do,” he said.
Grynkewich warned, “I want others to know who might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”
The theory of victory is structured around blocking, blunting and breaking an enemy — beginning with stymieing an initial attack and preventing an enemy advance by weakening it. Drawing on the final part of the theory, said Grynkewich, “we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”
Concentrating more on the warfighting elements to execute the new doctrine, he noted the “synchronized employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level” in order to “overwhelm enemy formations in contact.”
The end result would see enemy forces degraded to such an extent that they would be unable to continue an attack, explained Grynkewich.
“Across the alliance, we’re taking steps to operationalize this theory and maximize the readiness of our forces,” he made clear. “If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight.”
Grynkewich’s comments come as Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned today that NATO allies must be prepared to deal with a deadly Russian hybrid attack. Separately, when assessing the state of the Ukraine war, Grynkewich noted that the frontline has “largely stabilized” and that Russian long range attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, “probably” won’t break the will of the country’s civilian population.

5 Innovative Cars You Didn't Know Are the Vision of a Single Individual
42 photos
Photo: Volkswagen AG
No matter what thoughts you may have about the looks or performance of your favorite car or manufacturer, the vast majority of the automotive industry is in business thanks to more than just a handful of people.
For better or for worse, most cars come to exist thanks to the collective effort of thousands of engineers, designers, product planners, marketing executives, financial analysts, regulatory specialists and manufacturing experts. Their individual contributions are obviously compromised in one way or another at best, albeit they’re usually averaged and, in the end, committee-approved into the cars that end up in showrooms.
In other words, pretty much all modern cars are the result of the collective mind of a gigantic group of people rather than the vision of any specific individual inside that group, whether he is an engineer, a designer or the CEO of the actual company.
In other words, current cars are probably some of the most elaborate collaborative products in recent history, and attributing almost any of their features to any single person is, pretty much always, an over-simplification of the actual reality.
This description of the automotive state of affairs isn’t set in stone every single time, though. Mostly in the past, but sometimes in modern times as well, there has been a category of cars that defy all the expectations I mentioned above and can actually be attributed to the vision or creativity of a single person.
These cars are downright unicorns, since they’re as rare as hen’s teeth, but they do exist, and unsurprisingly, the way they came to exist is what makes them some of the coolest vehicles of any era. Probably even more interesting is that the minds that almost single-handedly created them sometimes worked against the wishes of the companies they worked for, or the expectations people had from those brands.
To put this thought into perspective, everyone expects a Ferrari to look cool and go fast, despite some of their cars not always being the quickest or the prettiest. Not everyone expected Volkswagen to unveil at one point a limited-edition, mid-engine hybrid diesel car with well under 100 horsepower and a six-figure price. Despite the German carmaker being a humongous organization, the Volkswagen XL1 and its previous iterations existed not thanks to a committee but to the vision of a single person, Ferdinand Piech.
The tear-shaped fuel-sipper from Wolfsburg is part of a select group of vehicles that never would have been created or sold to the public without the saying of a single individual. Without further ado, I decided to put together an exclusive list of some of these unique pieces of automotive history.
Some of the following cars were commercial failures that became cultural icons, while others were such a runaway success that it even confused their makers. What they all share is that they can trace their sheer existence to a single human being who refused to take no for an answer.
The Original Mini and Sir Alec Issigonis Very few cars can claim to have reshaped the entire automotive landscape, and the original Mini is one of them. As with the others on this list, the tiny British icon exists almost entirely because one man refused to accept that small cars had to be cramped, slow, and boring by default. That man was Alec Issigonis, a British-Greek engineer with a gift for thinking outside the box (pun intended) and a heavy distrust of the conventional.
It all started when the 1956 Suez Crisis sent fuel prices spiralling all over Europe, including the UK, which in turn gave the British Motor Corporation (BMC) a severe need for an inexpensive and very fuel-efficient small car to sell. At the time, the country’s streets had begun to be populated by German bubble cars, which were seen more like four-wheeled scooters with a roof than real cars by the chief of BMC.
Photo: MINI When Alec Issigonis was assigned the bubble car-fighter project, the brief stipulated that the model was supposed to be contained within a box that measured 10 by 4 by 4 feet (3.0 by 1.2 by 1.2 m), and that the passenger room should occupy approximately 6 feet (1.8 m) of the car’s 10-foot (3.0 m) length, or about 60 percent.
Starting from a blank sheet of paper and following the almost impossible brief, Issigonis implemented what was then seen as a radical solution. He turned the engine sideways, made the car front-wheel-drive, and pushed the wheels as far as possible to each four corners of the car. The result was a vehicle about as long as a bubble car, but which could carry four adults and their luggage.
The original Mini ’s compact transverse engine, FWD layout and thus its innovative packaging solutions instantly became the blueprint for pretty much all small city cars that have been developed since. What was initially just another shot at an economical runabout became a cultural icon. Everyone, from The Beatles to Steve McQueen drove one, and it even became a multiple rally winner after being modified by John Cooper.
The Shelby AC Cobra and Carroll Shelby While the original Mini was born to specifically solve a practical problem by an engineering genius and only became an icon as a side effect, the Cobra came to be out of the sheer lunacy and courage of Carroll Shelby. Unlike Sir Alec Issigonis, who was an engineer by trade, Shelby had a rather diverse career before eventually becoming a car builder.
He was a mildly successful chicken farmer until his farm went bankrupt and a successful racing car driver, even winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans and 1959, until a heart condition forced him to retire in 1960. Shelby then switched to building the cars we would enjoy racing, culminating a few years later with the Ferrari and world-beating Ford GT 40. Until then, he also accidentally created a new segment and one of the most legendary road-going sports cars of the 1960s in the form of the Shelby AC Cobra.
Photo: Shelby The Cobra’s origin story began in the UK, where a small company called AC Cars had been making a small and lightweight roadster called the Ace since the early 1950s. While the car was still competitive, its ancient Bristol engine, which had started as a BMW inline-six before World War II, was definitely falling behind regarding performance. At the same time, Ford had just developed a lightweight, all-aluminum 3.6-liter V8, and Shelby’s genius idea was to propose a marriage between the small British roadster and the American engine.
After the initial proposal was a success, Carroll Shelby pushed on and convinced AC to ship a bunch of Ace rolling chassis to California, where he promptly began dropping larger and larger Ford V8s in them, effectively creating the Shelby Cobra, and eventually the Cobra 427.
The resulting sports car was a perfect combination between European handling and American muscle that had never existed at this level before. It was so fast that it didn’t just compete with the Corvette or the Ferraris of its day, but it also beat them fair and square. It also became one of the best examples of how a small and almost unknown carmaker can fight with giants, and it was all thanks to one man, Carroll Shelby.
The McLaren F1 and Gordon Murray The F1 is arguably the best example of how a single individual’s vision can shape not only McLaren’t first-ever road car, but of how refusing to compromise can sometimes lead to the greatest ideas come to life. In fact, the only reason the McLaren F1 came to be was because of Gordon Murray’s obsession with specific engineering details that he either invented or insisted on using on the car.
Long before it was developed and subsequently unveiled, Murray had held almost the entirety of the parts comprising it in his mind. When he pitched the idea of a road car to McLaren boss Ron Dennis in the late 1980s, it was finally time for those thoughts to transcend into reality, no matter how extreme they were.
Photo: McLaren The actual idea behind the McLaren F1 was as radical as they get, which is probably why nobody had attempted it before. Murray wanted a three-seat sports car with the driver positioned centrally, like in a Formula 1 car, there were to be no compromises made on weight, and the car had to miss things like ABS and traction control, thus relying exclusively on mechanical grip and driver talent to be kept on the road.
The totality of Murray’s obsession for details is now legendary, but back then, it was borderline lunacy. Although he wanted the lightest possible car, which is why even the engine had to be naturally aspirated instead of turbocharged, he did specify a gold-plated engine bay. The metal was not chosen for its looks, and definitely not as a lightweight material, but gold is a great head reflector. The F1 also had bespoke titanium bolts to shave grams, and a custom lightweight audio system from Kenwood
Launched in 1992, the McLaren F1 rewrote all the rules in the supercar game, effectively becoming the first modern hypercar. It became the fastest production car in the world and its GTR version even won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1995, remaining the last road-car-derived vehicle to claim absolute victory at the famed endurance race. It was all made possible thanks to one man, Gordon Murray.
The Nissan GT-R (R35) and Kazutoshi Mizuno As mentioned before, it’s almost unheard of in modern times for a mainstream automaker to hand absolute authority over a car project to a single person, but that is exactly what happened with the Nissan GT-R (R35). Funnily enough, the story of its conception gets even cooler the more you learn about Kazutoshi Mizuno, the Chief Engineer for the project, and the model’s early development days.
Mizuno had worked for Nissan since 1972, and his resume already included things like overseeing the development of the R32 Skyline, running the carmaker’s Le Mans campaign and developing the 350Z. That said, when CEO Carlos Ghosn gave him almost total control over the GT-R (R35) it was something almost unheard of for such a large corporation. Kazutoshi Mizuno would answer to no one but the CEO, and he was in charge of every decision, starting with the engineering aspects and continuing with marketing, sales and future updates for the car.
Photo: Nissan Initially he wanted to turn down Ghosn’s offer, as Nissan executives had wanted to build the new GT-R on an existing platform, using a lot of shared parts. Completely rejecting the idea, arguing that it would betray the model’s flagship status, he eventually convinced Nissan to begin from a clean-sheet design and use a dedicated platform. He also championed an annual improvement strategy that looked at every model year as an evolution, which is why the R35 remained as competitive as ever from 2007 all the way to 2025.
What makes the model’s story even more remarkable is how in the early days of development, most of the engineers that worked on the transmission and suspension components had come from Isuzu’s truck division, and had no notion about creating a supercar. Instead of replacing them, Mizuno used 18 months to re-specialize them in two of the GT-R’s main technical attributes, including the innovative AWD chassis.
Not long after the model was unveiled, Kazutori Mizuno became a superstar, becoming known as the “Godfather of the GT-R” or simply “Mr GT-R,” and these were not exactly empty words. He literally supervised almost every single detail on the car’s technical development, and the GT-R would have never had the success it did if it weren’t for him.
The Volkswagen XL1 and Ferdinand Piech The only reason the Volkswagen XL1 actually existed as a (limited) production car is that Ferdinand Piech decided that a production car should be able to drive for 100 km (62 miles) using a single liter (0.26 gallons). Partly because he was a brilliant mechanical engineer by trade, partly because he was also a viciously good executive, the man simply refused to accept that it couldn’t be done.
As Volkswagen’s Chairman , Piech was famous for setting impossible targets and chasing impossible dreams, and the “one-liter car” was one of his personal obsessions. In 2002, over a decade before the XL1 entered production, he personally drove the earliest concept car for the model from Wolfsburg to Volkswagen’s annual shareholder meeting in Hamburg, while also showing that the one liter per 100 km (235 mpg) goal was achievable in the real world.
Photo: Volkswagen AG Of course, that achievement couldn’t be translated into production in that form, since the prototype that helped him do it was even more radical than its tear-drop shape implied. It was pretty much a highly aerodynamic engulfed moped, and was powered by a tiny single-cylinder diesel that developed 8.4 horsepower. The next order on Piech’s agenda was to make it fit for production, where it had to adhere to modern safety standards and be road legal in more than one jurisdiction, while seating two people and their luggage.
Following that impressive publicity stunt, Ferdinand Piech personally oversaw the project development’s, which slowly evolved through the L1 concept in 2009 and the XL1 concept in 2011, which finally reached production in 2013. The model was a technological marvel, weighing just 795 kg (1,752 pounds) thanks to using a carbon fiber monocoque chassis and various aluminum and magnesium parts. Its powertrain consisted of a 48-horsepower two-cylinder turbodiesel paired with a 27-horsepower electric motor and a 5.5 kWh battery.
Volkswagen reportedly invested around 1 billion euros into the project over the years, and the production XL1’s price was 111,000 Euros, with only 250 units being ever built. In other words, the car lost a lot of money for Volkswagen, but won tons of fans and respect for Ferdinand Piech in the process, since he showed one more time that he could bend an entire corporation to his vision.

The Smart #2 Premium. Image: smart
Smart is back in the two-seater business. The Mercedes-Benz and Geely joint venture unveiled the all-electric Smart #2 at the Paris Motor Show today, with a 35.8 kWh LFP battery, up to 290 km (180 miles) of WLTP range, and a starting price of €19,990.
That’s more than double the range of the last Smart EQ Fortwo, which never got DC fast charging. Early orders open in Europe tomorrow, and deliveries start in 2027.
The Fortwo formula, with the EV problems fixed
Smart picked the same Paris show where it revealed its first two-seater concept 30 years ago, and it didn’t mess with the recipe. The #2 is 2,746 mm long, about 5 cm longer than the old EQ Fortwo. The wheels are still pushed out to the corners, and the two-tone paint and split tailgate are back.
The turning circle is 6.95 meters curb-to-curb. Tiny.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The split tailgate carries over from the Fortwo. Image: smart
The big change is underneath. Smart developed a new platform for the car, which it calls Electric Compact Architecture (ECA), with the battery in the floor and a 60 kW motor driving the rear wheels with 130 Nm of torque. The company also claims the #2 has the first five-link rear suspension in its class.
The new Electric Compact Architecture (ECA) platform under the Smart #2. Image: smart
Here’s how it compares to the car it replaces. Power is identical. Almost everything else isn’t:
 | Smart EQ Fortwo (2020-2024) | Smart #2 (2027)
Battery | 17.6 kWh | 35.8 kWh LFP
WLTP range | 133 km | 290 km (target)
DC fast charging | None | 65 kW
AC charging | 4.6 kW (22 kW optional) | 7.4 kW / 11 kW
Motor | 60 kW | 60 kW
Length | 2,695 mm | 2,746 mm
EQ Fortwo figures from EV Database. Smart #2 figures from smart, pending EU homologation.
On a DC fast charger, Smart says the #2 goes from 10 to 80% in about 20 minutes. The base Pure trim is stuck with a 7.4 kW single-phase onboard charger, which takes about 5 hours for the same session, while the other trims get 11 kW. There’s also vehicle-to-load, but you need to buy a separate adapter for it.
The Smart #2 cabin, with an 8.8-inch driver display and a 10.1-inch center screen. Image: smart
Inside, there’s a bench-style seat layout, a 10.1-inch center screen, an 8.8-inch driver display, and an eight-year connectivity package. Adaptive cruise control with stop-and-go and Smart’s Pilot Assist are standard on every trim.
Four trims, starting at €19,990
Here’s the German pricing Smart released this afternoon. It says the €19,990 starting price also applies in France and Italy:
Pure: €19,990
Pure+: €20,990 (11 kW AC charging, heated driver seat)
Premium: €24,490 (glass roof, heated faux-leather seats, 7-speaker Sennheiser system)
Couture Edition: €25,690 (limited to 999 units in Europe)
Smart opened early orders at the Paris Motor Show with a starting price of 19,990 euros. Image: smart
Wolfgang Ufer, CEO of Smart Europe, said that “the time is right for the next chapter of the smart two-seater.” Smart is selling the car through its retail partners first, with online ordering following in the first half of 2027. The company notes the #2 is still going through EU homologation, so the specs could change before deliveries.
The timing makes sense. Mercedes handed half of Smart to Geely in 2019 and turned it into a Chinese-built EV brand, but so far that has meant crossovers like the #1, #3, and the Model Y-sized #5 . The #2 is the first car of the new era that looks like what people think of when they hear “Smart.”
The Twingo problem
The obvious rival is Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech, which also starts at €19,990 in Germany. The Twingo gets a 27.5 kWh LFP pack, up to 262 km of WLTP range, and 50 kW DC charging.
So the Smart wins on paper with 28 km more range and faster charging. But the Twingo has four seats and five doors for the same money.
And if you’re in the US, don’t get your hopes up. Daimler pulled Smart out of the US and Canada in 2019 , and a Chinese-built car with connected services has no path into the US market under current rules.
Electrek’s Take
We like this car. The original electric Fortwo was a great idea held back by its battery. With 133 km of WLTP range and no DC fast charging, it was a city car you couldn’t take out of the city and you’d need to think twice about buying it unless you had a charging situation at home in the city. Smart never solved that after launching the 17.6 kWh Fortwo electric drive in 2016. The #2 finally does, with twice the battery and a real fast-charging port.
Top comment by Beario
Liked by 3 people
Smart cars were never popular because the American market primarily focuses on cars with more room inside. Just have to look at the majority of cars sold here. It sounds great as a city car, but cities can be congested and expensive to find parking. The electric versions also do not have enough range to satisfy most people's range anxiety in the US. They will certainly sell some in Europe, but I am not sure how much because there are many options and increasing competition.
View all comments
But the price puts it in a tough spot. €19,990 is now the going rate for a small European EV, and at that price Renault gives you a four-seat hatchback. The two-seater’s argument has always been parking. In Paris, Rome, or Amsterdam, a car under 2.8 meters long can squeeze into spots nothing else fits, and that’s a real advantage. It’s also a niche one.
So the #2 will live or die on how many urban buyers value a tiny footprint over a back seat. The old Fortwo proved that market exists, but it was never huge. And Volkswagen’s ID. Every1 is supposed to land at around €20,000 in 2027, right when the #2 starts deliveries.
Still, this is the most compelling Smart in years. It’s a car with a clear purpose, which is more than we could say about the brand’s lineup of crossovers.

A state agency is providing a $1 million loan to add a rail spur connecting the Port of Columbia to Union Pacific ’s main line.
Louisiana Economic Development awarded the loan under its FastSites program, helping close a funding gap on the $7 million project.
The port, on a 400-acre site, has direct access to the Ouachita River and U.S. Route 165, and is adjacent to UP’s (NYSE: UNP)Monroe Subdivision. Columbia is about 30 miles south of Monroe, La.
“For a rural port like Columbia, FastSites provides critical gap financing that allows us to turn committed infrastructure funding into a project under construction,” Columbia Port Commission President Darron McGuffee said in a release. He pointed out that the project already has funding from the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development, as well as federal funding through the Delta Regional Authority’s Community Infrastructure Fund.
“The FastSites investment gives the port the financial flexibility needed to keep the project moving and maintain our construction schedule,” McGuffee said. “More importantly, this rail spur will provide public access to Union Pacific’s main line for our region, creating new transportation opportunities for existing businesses while strengthening our ability to attract future industrial investment like Louisiana Green Fuels.”
“ Adding rail access at the Port of Columbia opens another path for businesses across Northeast Louisiana to move goods and reach markets,” state Sen. Glen Womack said. “That kind of connectivity strengthens our ability to support the industries already operating here while creating more possibilities for companies looking to invest in the region.”
The port expects to open the project for bids in November. Construction is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and be completed by 2028.

One year ago, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll eviscerated bureaucratic delay and acquisition roadblocks in a profanity-laced public address .
On Monday, his successor, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle , took things back to the biblical book of Genesis in his first public speech to troops since assuming the role.
“Controlling land is fundamental to humanity,” he told a packed ballroom at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting . “The Army does it better than anyone, and it’s on us, the people in this room, to keep it that way. Humanity’s connection to the land is biblical, and it even transcends faith, since the dawn of creation, as recorded in Genesis.”
Telle, who previously served as the assistant secretary of the Army for public works, enlisted the Old Testament to preach a message of simplicity of purpose, invoking the sacred ground of past battlefields and the Army’s long history of protecting American territory.
“It makes me wonder why the United States Army, again the most lethal and dominant institution in human history, struggles to explain in common terms who we are in 2026, who we really are,” Telle said. “We’ve drowned ourselves and the public in buzzwords, strategies, slideshows, government acronyms and bureaucratic doublespeak — things that are advertised as revolutionary. But the Army’s value proposition is actually too fundamental for goofy corporate jargon.”
Though Telle’s rhetorical approach differed from Driscoll’s, he quickly made it clear that the Army was holding the course set by his predecessor, who resigned Aug. 31 over growing disagreements and friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Adam Telle, acting secretary of the Army, poses for an official portrait on Sept. 15, 2026 (William Pratt/U.S. Army)
Telle hailed the Army’s work to streamline acquisition and reduce roadblocks to getting soldiers the gear they need, citing the Army’s work to reduce service “fiefdoms” from thousands to a few newly named portfolio acquisition executives.
The service, he said, is moving away from what he called “compound self-interest,” or bureaucratic risk avoidance.
“We’re empowering a small number of teams to address our biggest mandates to make difficult trade-offs around speed, manufacturability and supply chain realities early, often and together,” he said. “This is how you generate compound soldier-interest. That’s the opposite of compound self-interest.”
He demonstrated the Pentagon’s new small drones online marketplace , likening it to Amazon.com and showing how soldiers could access it on their smartphones and leave reviews for future soldiers based on how well their gear worked.
Likewise, he compared the Army’s new online test range reservation system for industry, initiated under Driscoll, to the hotel reservation site Booking.com .
The site, he said, is like a “white-glove concierge service that allows innovators to get a reservation on the range faster.”
Officials have previously said the new system can accelerate companies’ range-testing schedules from as much as 18 months to 30 days.
Telle also reasserted the Army’s commitment to what the military has called a “right to repair,” meaning that it will demand open-architecture systems from all future vendors and limit industry’s ability to control intellectual property and charge a premium for fixes and spare parts.
“Right now, we’re sprinting to field low-cost interceptors with open architecture built in from the outset. We need these low-cost interceptors to shoot down missiles and drones headed our way,” Telle said. “We know we need thousands of these things, but they have to seamlessly connect to our network.
“If the data is trapped behind proprietary moats, and we have to call a contractor to decode the data, our superintelligent command and control doesn’t matter,” He continued. “Everything we buy from here on out will have open architecture; it’s non-negotiable.”
A ‘manufacturing rodeo’
Next, he said, the Army will launch a new project: a “manufacturing rodeo,” to be held early next year, that will put the service’s industrial base suppliers in competition with each other.
“We’ve invested a lot in our organic industrial base. Now we need to strain it in the nation’s larger industrial base,” Telle said. “We’re going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes and see where it breaks.”
Telle did not provide specifics, such as the precise mechanism for competition or the challenges in which companies would be asked to compete.
“We’re going to learn by doing, not by sitting around postulating at the Pentagon,” he said. “We’re going to find the weak links. We’re going to make them stronger, and we’re going to keep iterating.”
Telle did not refer to Driscoll or allude to the fact that the service has no current Army secretary nominee. He did, however, address the “beautifully chaotic” system of American government, saying that while it wasn’t efficient, it centered human freedom and allowed for creativity and innovation.
“The United States Army laid the groundwork for that, and will continue to guarantee that it’s never extinguished. Meanwhile, the other team’s human spirit, its imagination, is bounded and boxed and regulated,” Telle said. “The United States of America is where the magic happens, where brilliant people turn science fiction into science fact, and you can’t flip a switch to turn that on.
“The Army’s work over the course of history has been so fundamental, so successful that the American spirit it unleashed is now the most important and potent force we have,” he continued. “It’s a potent force that the other guys don’t have.”

Half of US-Market BMW M2 Coupe Buyers Want a Manual Whose Future Remains Uncertain
